lessons.title: नाम (nāma) — "name," the source of a word half the world shares

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The first word of the introduction — and, since this is Sanskrit, the source of the word half the world uses.
न (na) + ा (the long-ā sign) + म (ma) becomes नाम (nāma).

नाम (nāma, "name," neuter) is from the stem नामन् (nāman), from Proto-Indo-European h₃nómn̥. This is not a borrowing from anywhere — it is the ancestor: the same root surfaces as English name, Latin nōmen ( becomes noun, nominate), Greek onoma, and, worn down, as Hindi nām, Bengali nām, Punjabi nāṁ. When you say Sanskrit nāma, you are standing near the headwaters of a word that flowed to both Europe and modern India.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: its children, west and east — English *name*, Latin *nōmen*; Hindi *nām*]

segments.text: What PIE root is nāma from, and name two of its descendants. (h₃nómn̥; any two of English name, Latin nōmen, Greek onoma, Hindi nām.)

lessons.title: मम (mama) — "my," the ancestor of me and my

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The word that makes the name yours — and it is, quite literally, the grandparent of English my.
म (ma) + म (ma) becomes मम (mama). Two identical syllables.

मम (mama, "my, of me") is the genitive of अहम् (aham, "I"), on the first-person root ma-, from Proto-Indo-European me-. This is the source of the whole first-person family: English me, my, mine, Latin meus, Greek emou, and Hindi merā. Sanskrit mama and English my are not merely similar — they are the same ancient word, one still in its old form, the other worn smooth by five thousand years.

segments.instruction: "mama"
the m- family — mama / English me, my / Latin meus / Hindi merā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the m- family — *mama* / English *me*, *my* / Latin *meus* / Hindi *merā*]

segments.text: What is mama the genitive of, and its English cousins? (Aham, "I"; English me, my, mine.)

lessons.gloss: the single character ◌ः — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌ः and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one, the ones you have already met: न, द, ◌्. Say what each of them does.
One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a visarga: not a letter, but a soft breathed ḥ at the end of a syllable. It is the mark that ends a great many Sanskrit masculine nouns, so it is worth knowing on sight.
Where it sits: a pair of dots to the right of the syllable, marking a voiceless post-vocalic breath.
Worked through: न + ◌ः = नः — naḥ.
You already say these words, and ◌ः (ḥ) is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:
namaskāraḥ — hello (lit. "the making of a bow").
dhanyavādaḥ — thank you.
Put your pen on ◌ः (ḥ) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: अस्ति (asti) — "is," the ancestor of is and est

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The little verb "is" — and here you meet it in the form that fathered half the "to be" words on earth.
अ (independent a) + स्ति (sti, the conjunct स् s + ति ti) becomes अस्ति (asti).

अस्ति (asti, "is") is the third-person singular of the root अस् (as-, "to be"), from Proto-Indo-European h₁es-. It is the source of the family's copula: English is, German ist, Latin est, Greek esti, and Hindi hai ( from asti directly). Unlike its Dravidian neighbours — Tamil and Bengali drop "is" in the present — Sanskrit keeps an explicit copula, and it is the very word Europe kept too.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the family — *asti* / English *is* / Latin *est* / Greek *esti* / Hindi *hai*]

segments.text: What root is asti from, and its cousins across the family? (As- / PIE h₁es-; English is, Latin est, Hindi hai.)

lessons.title: मम नाम … अस्ति (mama nāma … asti) — "my name is…"

segments.text: Three atoms you now own, assembled — and note that Sanskrit, unlike Tamil or Bengali, actually says the "is."
मम (my) + नाम (name) + your name + अस्ति (is) = mama nāma … asti, "my name is…" Mama nāma Aruṇaḥ asti. becomes "My name is Arun."

Where Tamil says only eṉ peyar Arun and Bengali āmār nām Arun — both dropping the verb (the zero copula) — Sanskrit says मम नाम … अस्ति (mama nāma … asti), with an explicit asti ("is"). This is the Indo-European way, the one Latin and English kept too (my name is …). The verb comes last, as in the modern Indian languages that descend from it. (In casual use asti can be dropped, but the "full-dress" Sanskrit sentence keeps it.)

lessons.title: आ (ā) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character आ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: आ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one, the ones you have already met: द, ◌्, ◌ः (ḥ). Say what each of them does.
One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
आ — ā.
It is an independent vowel: the full-size letter a vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. Inside a word the same vowel is written as a small sign instead.
What it is made of:
the joined upper-and-lower left body of a.
a middle shoulder.
an inner vertical stem.
a trailing vertical stem.
the top shirorekhā.
You already say this word, and आ (ā) is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:
ām / na — yes / no.
1. curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting.
2. lift and sweep the middle shoulder right.
3. lift and draw the inner stem top-to-bottom.
4. lift and draw the trailing stem top-to-bottom.
5. lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right.
Pen lifts: 4. The pen comes up 4 times and no more.
verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the shared a body into more strokes.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ (ā) stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.

lessons.title: भवान् / त्वम् (bhavān / tvam) — "you," respectful and familiar

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: To ask a name you need "you" — and Sanskrit's familiar one is the ancestor of English thou.
त्वम् (tvam): त्व (the conjunct tva) + म् (bare m, closed by the halant). भवान् (bhavān): भ + वा + न्.

त्वम् (tvam, familiar "you") is from Proto-Indo-European tū — the direct ancestor of English archaic thou, Latin tū, French tu, and Hindi tū. भवान् (bhavān, respectful "you") is different: it is really a third-person honorific — "your honour," from bhavat ("being, gracious one") — and so it takes a third-person verb (bhavān asti, "your honour is"), a politeness by grammatical distance. For a first meeting, use भवान्.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: politeness by grammatical person

segments.text: Where Hindi and Punjabi make respect plural (āp … haiṁ), Sanskrit makes it third-person: to be polite you address someone as though speaking about them — "is your honour well?" rather than "are you well?" Different trick, same courtesy.

segments.instruction: "tvam" (familiar) and "bhavān" (respectful)
the English cousin of tvam (thou)
why bhavān takes a third-person verb (it means "your honour")
segments.source: [YOU SAY: why *bhavān* takes a third-person verb (it means "your honour")]

segments.text: Which "you" is respectful, and what English word is tvam cousin to? (Bhavān — literally "your honour," taking a 3rd-person verb; tvam corresponds to archaic thou.)

lessons.title: किम् (kim) — "what," the source of the question-words

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The question-word — and the fountainhead of a whole family of "wh-" words, east and west.
कि (ki, क + the i-sign) + म् (bare m, with the halant) becomes किम् (kim).

किम् (kim, "what") is from the interrogative stem क- (ka-), from Proto-Indo-European kʷo- — the ancestor of the whole question-family: English what, who, which, Latin quis / quid, Greek tis, and Hindi kyā / kaun. Sanskrit's own questions all grow from this ka-: kim (what), kaḥ (who), kadā (when), kutra (where), katham (how). It is the single seed from which both Europe's qu-/wh- words and India's k- words grew.

lessons.title: भ (bha) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character भ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: भ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one, the ones you have already met: ◌्, ◌ः (ḥ), आ (ā). Say what each of them does.
One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
भ — bha.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not bh, it is bha.
What it is made of:
a clockwise upper loop joined to a descending trunk.
a clockwise lower bowl continuing through a rightward crossbar.
a top-to-bottom right stem.
the top shirorekhā.
You already say this word, and भ (bha) is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:
bhavān / tvam — you.

1. start at the upper loop's lower inner tip, sweep left and clockwise around the upper loop, descend the joined trunk, curl clockwise around the lower bowl, and continue right through the crossbar without lifting.
2. lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom.
3. lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right.
Pen lifts: 2. The pen comes up 2 times and no more.
verified three-stroke teaching form; another learner source stages the upper and lower body parts separately.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari bʰ भ (bha).gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009.

lessons.title: तव नाम किम्? (tava nāma kim?) — "what's your name?"

segments.text: Turn the introduction around — ask, instead of tell.

तव (tava, "your," the genitive of tvam) + नाम (name) + किम् (what) becomes "your name what?" Here Sanskrit often drops the asti: tava nāma kim? stands complete, the question-word alone doing the work.

Tava ("your") is the familiar form, matching tvam. To a respected stranger, use the honorific: भवतः नाम किम्? (bhavataḥ nāma kim? — bhavataḥ, "of your honour"). Note mama / tava / bhavataḥ — "my / your / your-honour's" — all built the same way, as genitives.

lessons.title: आनन्दः (ānandaḥ) — "joy," and "a joy to meet you"
lessons.gloss: joy — and "meeting you is a joy"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The warm close of an introduction — a word so full it names bliss itself.
आ (independent ā) + न + न्द (the conjunct nda) + ः (the visarga ḥ, the masculine-singular ending you met in Chapter 1) becomes आनन्दः (ānandaḥ).

To say "pleased to meet you," Sanskrit can say भवन्तं दृष्ट्वा आनन्दः (bhavantaṁ dṛṣṭvā ānandaḥ) — "seeing you, [there is] joy." The key word आनन्दः (ānandaḥ, "joy, bliss, delight") is from आ- (ā-, "fully") + the root नन्द् (nand, "to rejoice"). It is one of Sanskrit's most beloved words — the ānanda of sat-cit-ānanda ("being-consciousness-bliss"), and the name Ānanda, the Buddha's devoted disciple. So a simple greeting reaches for the word Indian thought uses for the deepest happiness.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
Where it sits: a curl placed BEFORE (to the left of) the consonant, though pronounced after.
Worked through: न + ◌ि = नि — ni.
You already say these words, and ◌ि is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:
asti — is.
mama nāma … asti — my name is…
kim — what.
tava nāma kim? — what's your name?
Put your pen on ◌ि and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
